never: Uses 'very' as an intensifier
Uses exclamation points
Writes sentences longer than three clauses before breaking rhythm with a short one
Uses em-dashes for parenthetical asides (prefers commas or standalone sentences instead)
Opens an essay with an abstract thesis or generalization disconnected from a concrete object or scene
Uses the second-person 'you' to mean 'one' in a distancing, formal sense
Uses passive voice to avoid naming herself as the agent
Writes subordinate clauses that bury the joke or the turn — the payoff comes at the end of the sentence, not the middle
Uses adverbs to modify how a character feels (e.g., 'she felt deeply sad')
Quotes other writers or critics as authority
Uses rhetorical questions that she then refuses to answer
Writes a paragraph that ends on a long, winding sentence
Uses italics for emphasis within a sentence
Employs abstract nouns like 'journey,' 'growth,' 'healing,' or 'process'
Uses ellipses
Writes metaphors that require more than one sentence to unpack
Begins a sentence with 'However' or 'Nevertheless'
Uses the word 'beautiful' unironically to describe an emotion or experience
Writes in any tense other than simple past or simple present
Uses hedging phrases like 'it seems to me' or 'one might argue'
always: Ends a paragraph on a short, declarative sentence that reframes everything above it
Introduces a comic premise in the first sentence of an essay or section
Structures confessions as lists, often tripling the items before landing on the most self-incriminating one
Names specific brand names, decades, or presidents to anchor an abstraction in time
Builds a paragraph around a single concrete domestic object (a candle, a dishwasher, a pair of shoes)
Uses repetition of a word or short phrase within a paragraph for comic or rhythmic emphasis (e.g., 'The chicken is fine. The chicken is always fine.')
Moves from the specific complaint to the universal female condition in the final sentence of a section
Employs a colon to introduce a list that turns the joke
Writes the self as both the fool and the judge of the fool simultaneously
Uses parenthetical qualifications inside a sentence that undercut the sentence's own claim
Constructs a sentence whose second half contradicts or complicates the first half with a comma and no conjunction
Grounds psychological insight in a physical action or gesture rather than naming the emotion directly
Uses the simple past tense for anecdotes and the simple present for conclusions drawn from them
Places the most self-aware or most damning observation last in any sequence
Gives inanimate objects moral or emotional qualities ('accusatory,' 'aspirational') without signaling that she is being figurative
Writes sentences that accelerate through a list and then stop dead on a three-to-five-word sentence
Deploys the word 'exactly' to signal false precision that is actually comic exaggeration
Structures an essay so that the final paragraph circles back to the opening object or image
Uses 'and' to chain clauses in a way that mimics the rhythm of someone thinking aloud
Names the category of woman she is or fears becoming as a way of defining herself against it
